title: the incr/decr rewrite copies three bytes of a two-byte terminator, one byte past the item's data
live_proof: absent at the pin: 1.6.45:memcached.c:2317 reads 'memcpy(ITEM_data(new_it) + res, "\r\n", 2);' -- the fixed length -- immediately after 'memcpy(ITEM_data(new_it), buf, res);' at :2316, so the site survives verbatim with the fix applied. A fix-reversal. The defect was INTRODUCED by c47ee89 (2007, 'fix potential bug with memcpy()', which changed the length from 2 to 3) and fixed by 2d61f18 (2008); both halves of that pair are in history, which is how the shape was confirmed rather than inferred.
object: an item's data field, sized exactly res + 2 by do_item_alloc
lifetime_ender: NONE -- the item is alive throughout. The corpus's first SPATIAL row.
shape: one byte written past an item's data into the next chunk of the page
allocator_layer: slabs.c chunks over 1 MiB pages, memcached 1.6.45
fidelity: model-consumer, real allocator. Two chunks come from the real slab allocator and the item's data is sized to end exactly at the measured chunk STRIDE -- derived from the distance between the two chunks, not from any assumed class size -- so the one-byte overflow crosses the CHUNK bound rather than landing in the class's rounding slack. That is the reachable worst case.
distinguishing: the only row here whose crossing leaves the chunk, so it is the one a chunk-granular bound could catch. MEASURED only natively. The chunk bound is what the slab port narrows (leases.c carves each chunk), so whether a Capstone arm faults depends on whether this crossing leaves the CHUNK or stays inside it -- stated per case below and NOT measured here: the domain arms need a build this run did not make.

spatial.note: PREDICTION CONFIRMED by the run of 2026-10-05. It was filed as a prediction before any domain build existed, and the reading matches. The crossing LEAVES the chunk, so the slab port's chunk bound catches it -- and the cause is 7, a bounds violation on a STORE, not the load fault's 5. Measured on BOTH modes: the spatial arm faults too, so the slab port narrows per chunk whatever the temporal mode, exactly as wm_narrow() does on the wireshark side. Judged on the unprotected spatial mode.

native-detect.oracle: MEASURED 2026-10-09, results/2026-10-09-native-asan/: **NO ASan REPORT** on the buggy arm, which printed VERDICT DEFECT-REPRODUCED, so the defective access ran and ASan did not see it. The fixed arm exits 0 with VERDICT FIXED and no report. Built with the port's own allocator library under the same sanitizer (cc (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0; -fsanitize=address -fno-omit-frame-pointer -O1 -g; port library with the same sanitizer). Positive controls in the same run: `asan-control past 67108864` -> heap-buffer-overflow; `asan-control uaf 67108864` -> heap-use-after-free -- so ASan reports on a heap block the size of this corpus's arena, and the silence is the arena: one malloc'd block, carved and recycled without free(). Predicted before the run (3ef5169ae90b); the arm was previously 'declined'.
native-detect.note: DECLINED, not pending, and the reason is a measurement rather than an estimate: the two-sided shape is already established by the FFmpeg sub-object probe (ffmpeg/subobject-repros/results/20261005-native-subobject/asan-probe.c), where the member-to-member crossing draws NO report while a write one element past the whole allocation draws heap-buffer-overflow. Every crossing in this corpus stays inside one g_malloc'd block or slab page by the same mechanism, so eight more silent-with-control runs would confirm what one already showed. Two further reasons not to spend them: the wireshark corpus has no standalone native build to instrument, and the memcached one would have to instrument the case while linking an uninstrumented port library -- the mixed mode in which that probe's own -O1 artefact arose, where BOTH arms went silent because the dead stores were optimised away. If this arm is ever wanted, it needs its positive control in the same binary.
